text: k-means asks you to choose k first. Hierarchical clustering flips that around — it builds a complete family tree of your data, from every row alone up to a single group containing everything, and you decide afterward where to cut the tree. That makes it a great exploration tool, and some variants handle cases where k-means fails.

Agglomerative clustering starts with every row as its own cluster. At each step it merges the two closest clusters, repeating until only one remains — with 300 customers, that's 299 merges. The result is a dendrogram, a tree whose branch heights show how far apart groups were at the moment they joined. Tall jumps mean you merged two very different groups.

Distance between two single points is clear, but distance between two clusters needs a rule, called linkage. Ward merges the pair that increases within-cluster variance the least, producing compact groups, similar to k-means — it's the scikit-learn default. Complete uses the farthest pair, average uses the mean distance, and single uses the closest pair, which can follow long chained shapes.

Building the tree on our seeded customers with Ward linkage: the result has shape 299 by 4, one row per merge. The last three merge distances are 4.31, 22.46, and 24.31 — the last two merges join big, distant groups, and they're much taller than the merge right before them. That jump is the tree telling you there are three natural groups.

Cutting the tree at 3 clusters with fcluster gives exactly 100, 100, and 100 — matching the real groups perfectly. The scikit-learn version, AgglomerativeClustering, fits the same workflow as other estimators, giving the same counts and a silhouette score of 0.773, identical to k-means here because these blobs are clean.

Drawing the dendrogram for the last 12 merges makes the structure visible directly. And here's where linkage really matters — on two interlocking crescents, single linkage splits them exactly right, 150 and 150, while Ward gives 184 and 116, cutting across them just as k-means did.

Hierarchical clustering compares many pairs of rows, so it needs memory and time that grow quickly — comfortable for thousands of rows, painful for millions. It also can't undo a merge once made. Use it for exploration on modest data, when you want structure at several levels, and when cluster shapes are irregular.

Use k-means instead when the dataset is large. To recap: agglomerative clustering merges the closest groups again and again into a dendrogram, and you cut the tree to get clusters. The linkage rule defines closest — ward for compact groups, single for chained shapes. Next, a different kind of unsupervised learning: shrinking many columns into a few with PCA.
